support.locus: Il. 8.88; Il. 8.254 (35 Homeric lines with ὠκύς + ἵππος)

cognate: *HoHḱu- 'swift' + *h₁éḱwo- 'horse': Ved. āśú- áśva-, Gk ὠκέες ἵπποι, Av. āsu.aspa- (compound)
drift_or_renewal: In Vedic āśú- is often used alone as a noun meaning '(swift) horse' (RV 2.31.2c āśávaḥ; 2.34.3b āśúbhiḥ, with áśvān in the line before); Avestan has it only in the bahuvrīhi āsu.aspa-.
shared_syntax: attributive adjective + noun (Gk ὠκέες ἵπποι; Ved. āśúm áśvam), or the adjective used as a noun
context: Chariot horses running: the Maruts' horses at the race (ājíṣu) in RV 2.34.3; the swift ones pulling the chariot across the air in RV 2.31.2; Rhesus' horses tethered by the chariot in Il. 10.474. The noun-epithet pair is fixed in both traditions (35 Homeric lines; several RV pādas) and also turns up in an Avestan compound, so it is a formula, not a chance pairing.

support.locus: Aesch. PV 91; Soph. Ant. 416; Eur. Hec. 412; Eur. El. 465

cognate: *sóh₂wl̥ / *sh₂wén- 'sun' + *kʷékʷlo- 'wheel': Ved. sū́ra-/sū́rya- cakrá-, Gk ἡλίου κύκλος, ON (sól =) fagrahvél
drift_or_renewal: Greek κύκλος has broadened to 'circle, disc', but in Eur. Ion 41 the sun 'riding' (ἱππεύοντος ἡλίου κύκλῳ) keeps the image of a vehicle; in Old Norse the wheel survives only in the compound kenning fagrahvél 'fair wheel'.
shared_syntax: genitive of 'sun' + 'wheel' (Ved. sū́ryasya cakrám, cakrám ... sū́ram; Gk ἡλίου κύκλος)
context: The sun pictured as a wheel or chariot crossing the sky: Indra tearing off the sun's wheel (RV 1.130.9, 1.175.4); the 'bright wheel of the sun' blazing with its rays (Aesch. Pers. 504) and the sun's riding wheel (Eur. Ion 41). Poetic, cosmological language in all three traditions. In Ion 42 the words stand in the context line (41).

support.locus: Il. 15.46 (πατὴρ ἀνδρῶν τε θεῶν τε); 41 Homeric lines with Ζεύς + πατήρ

cognate: *dyéw- + *ph₂tér-: Ved. dyaúṣ pitā́, Gk Ζεῦ πάτερ (cf. Lat. Iuppiter, from outside the slab)
drift_or_renewal: Vedic dyaúḥ is still the sky deified and is paired with Earth as mother (pr̥thivī́ mātā́); in Greek Ζεύς is a personal god and the pair is a fixed vocative of address
shared_syntax: divine name + 'father' in apposition (Ved. nominative predicate 'Heaven is your father'; Gk vocative Ζεῦ πάτερ)
context: Address or description of the sky-god as father in a prayer or invocation. Thetis praying to Zeus (Il. 1.504); the Vedic charm naming Heaven as father and Earth as mother (RV 1.191.6). Both words stand in the context lines of their passages.

cognate: *HoHḱu- 'swift' + *peth₂- 'fly': Ved. āśupátvan- / āśúbhiḥ pátasi ~ Gk ὠκυπέτης / ὠκείῃς πτερύγεσσι
drift_or_renewal: Greek has the verbal root as the noun πτέρυξ 'wing' in the free phrase and as -πέτης only in the compound; Vedic keeps the finite verb (pátasi). The compound in each language (āśupátvan- of the falcon, ὠκυπέτης of horses) shows the collocation was fixed.
shared_syntax: 'swift' qualifying the means or the subject of flying: āśúbhiḥ (instrumental) pátasi ~ ὠκείῃς πτερύγεσσι (instrumental dative); compound adjective in both
context: Fast flight of divine beings: Indra flying many leagues with his swift (horses) in RV 2.16.3; the Harpies following the winds and birds 'with swift wings' (Hes. Th. 269); the bee-maidens of h.Herm. 553; Zeus' eagle in Pind. P. 1.6. Homer's ὠκυπέτα is said of horses, as in the Vedic pāda, which makes the parallel with RV 2.16.3 closer.

cognate: *yewg-/*yugóm + *gʷṓws with Dawn as subject: Ved. (uṣā́ḥ) yuṅkté gávām ~ Gk ἠώς ... ἐπὶ ζυγὰ βουσὶ τίθησιν
drift_or_renewal: Greek replaces the verb 'yoke' (Ved. yuj-) with a phrase built on the noun: ζυγὰ ... τίθησιν 'puts yokes on'. In Vedic the cows are Dawn's own mythic team (red cows = rays); in Hesiod the image is agricultural: Dawn makes men yoke their oxen.
shared_syntax: Dawn (subject) + 'yoke' + cattle (Ved. genitive gávām / accusative gā́ḥ; Gk dative βουσί)
context: What daybreak brings: in RV 1.124.11 Dawn rises in the east and yokes the array of red cows; in Hes. Op. 578-581 Dawn, appearing, sets many men on the road and puts yokes on oxen. Dawn as yoker of cattle is the shared figure. Hesiod's version may be the realia behind the Vedic myth, but in both the action belongs to Dawn herself.

cognate: *séno- 'old' + *néwo- 'new' as a polar pair: Ved. sánā návā ca (RV 8.45.25), sánā ... návyāḥ ~ Gk ἕνη καὶ νέα
drift_or_renewal: In Greek the pair has become a calendar term ('old and new [day]', the last day of the month), and ἕνος 'old' survives almost only in this phrase. That makes it a frozen relic. In Vedic it is a live merism for deeds or things old and new.
shared_syntax: two cognate adjectives coordinated (Ved. sánā návā ca; Gk ἕνη τε καὶ νέα); in RV 1.174.8a the two are predicative ('the old [deeds] have come as new')
context: The contexts differ (Vedic praise of Indra's deeds, old and renewed; Attic dating of the month's turn), so the match rests on the pairing alone. 'Old and new' is a natural polar pair and could have been coined independently. The weight of the claim is that Greek kept the otherwise lost *séno- only inside this binomial.

cognate: *peth₂- 'spread out' for opening doors, together with *kleh₂w- 'bar, key': Lat. claustra pandite ianuae ~ Gk κληΐδι πετάσθησαν (θύρετρα)
drift_or_renewal: The door noun is renewed (Lat. ianua; Gk θύρετρα/θύρα, whose cognate Lat. fores is not used here); the bolt/key word and the verb are cognate
shared_syntax: verb *peth₂- with the door (or its bars) as object (Latin imperative, active) or as subject (Greek passive), with the *kleh₂w- bolt/key mentioned in the same clause
context: Opening a house's double doors: the bride's arrival in Catullus' wedding hymn ('open the bars of the door'); Penelope unlocking the storeroom, where the doors fly open when struck by the key (Od. 21.47-50). Both languages also have the commoner verbs aperio / ἀνοίγω, which makes the shared choice of *peth₂- notable. Still, 'spread open' for folding doors is an easy metaphor to coin independently.

note: All 188 bundles read in 10 sections. 7 claims: 3 high (swift horses; wheel of the sun; Father Sky/Zeus pater, the last in context lines only), 2 medium (swift-flying; Dawn yokes cattle), 2 low (old-and-new merism; *peth2- + *kleh2w- door opening). Rejected as generic or incongruent: 'fire burns' (agni/ignis + *h1ews-), animal lists, drive cows (*h2eg-), urvi/bahula ~ eureiai/pakheiai, potnia meter ~ AV mataram ... patnim, madhu pa- ~ methyo.
